(p-251) Surah 63: Al-Munafiqun

Medinan, and its verses are eleven.

﴿When the hypocrites come to you﴾, i.e., they attend your assembly.

﴿They say, "We bear witness that you are indeed the Messenger of Allah."﴾ They emphasize their statement with "inna" (indeed) and the lam (emphatic lam), to signal that this testimony of theirs issues from the core of their hearts, the sincerity of their belief, and the abundance of their desire and eagerness. His words, Exalted is He, ﴿And Allah knows that you are indeed His Messenger﴾, are a parenthetical clause (i'tirad, interjection) confirming the explicit content of their speech. It is placed between this and His words, Exalted is He, ﴿And Allah bears witness that the hypocrites are indeed liars﴾, to establish and specify what the charge of lying is attached to, namely that they said it out of belief, as has been indicated, and to remove at the outset what might be suspected of the lie being directed at the explicit content of their speech. That is: "And Allah bears witness that they are indeed liars in what they implied by their statement, namely that it issues from belief and peace of heart." The use of the explicit noun in place of the pronoun is to censure them and to indicate the cause of the ruling.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 63, verse 2:

﴿They have taken their oaths as a shield﴾, the false oaths, of which is what is related about them.

﴿A shield (junnah)﴾, i.e., a protection against what would come upon them of being held to account by killing and taking captive, or otherwise. Taking them as a shield is an expression for their preparing and readying them for the time of need, so that they may swear by them and be freed from being held to account, not for actually using them, since that comes after being held to account, which is preceded by the commission of the crime. And the taking of a shield must be before being held to account, and on account of its cause as well, as the particle fa' (then/so) in His, exalted is He, saying reveals: ﴿and so they barred (others) from the way of Allah﴾, i.e., they barred those who wished to enter Islam by saying that he, upon him be prayers and peace, is not a messenger, and those who wished to spend in the way of Allah by forbidding it, as will be related of them. There is no doubt that this barring on their part preceded their swearing in deed. It is also read "their faith (iman)", i.e., what they manifested on their tongues, so taking it as a shield is an expression for using it in deed, for it protects them, unlike their blood and their property. The meaning of His, exalted is He, saying ﴿so they barred﴾ then is: they persisted in what they were upon of barring and turning away from His way, exalted is He.

﴿Indeed, evil is what they used to do﴾, of hypocrisy and barring. In "evil (saa')" there is the sense of wonder and magnifying the matter of them in the eyes of the listeners.

That (ﷺ) — correction: "That" refers back to what has preceded: the declaration against them that they are the worst of people in their deeds, or to what He has described of their state of hypocrisy, lying, and concealing disbelief behind outward faith. The demonstrative (dhalika, "that") carries the sense of distance, despite the nearness of the reference, as has been noted repeatedly before, indicating the remoteness of their rank in evil.

﴿Because﴾ i.e., due to the fact that they

﴿believed﴾ i.e., they uttered the testimony of faith, like all who enter Islam.

﴿then disbelieved﴾ i.e., their disbelief became manifest through the signs and indications of unbelief that were observed from them; or, they professed belief in the presence of the believers, then professed disbelief in the presence of their devils.

﴿so a seal was set upon their hearts﴾ until they became accustomed to disbelief and were at ease with it. It is also read in the active voice, and it is read "so God sealed" (fa-tabaʿa Allāh).

﴿so they do not understand﴾ the reality of faith, and they do not know its reality at all.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 63, verse 4:**

﴿And when you see them, their bodies please you﴾ due to their largeness, and their appearance delights you due to the brightness of their faces.

﴿And if they speak, you listen to their speech﴾ due to their eloquence, the fluency of their tongues, and the sweetness of their speech. Ibn Ubayy was a large-bodied and eloquent man who would attend the assembly of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ along with a group of his like, who were the leaders of Madinah. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ and those with him would be impressed by their physiques and would listen to their speech. It has also been said: the address is to everyone who is fit to be addressed. This is supported by the reading "yusma'" (is listened to) in the passive voice, and by His statement, exalted is He, ﴿As if they were propped-up pieces of wood﴾, which is in the position of nominative as the predicate of an omitted subject, or as an independent statement with no place in the i'rab. They were likened, in their sitting in the gatherings of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, leaning against them, to upright pieces of wood propped against a wall, in that they were bodies empty of knowledge and good. It is also read "khushbun" (khushb), as the plural of khashabah (a piece of wood), like budn, the plural of badanah. It has been said that it is the plural of khashba', which is a piece of wood whose inside has rotted, meaning corrupted; they were likened to it in their hypocrisy and the corruption of their inner selves. It is also read "khashab," like madarah and madar.

﴿They think every cry is against them﴾, that is, falling upon them, harmful to them, because of their cowardice and the settling of terror in their hearts. It has been said: they were apprehensive that Allah would send down something about them that would expose their concealments and make their blood and property lawful.

﴿They are the enemy﴾, that is, they are the complete and firmly established ones in enmity, for the worst of enemies is the smiling enemy who flatters you while beneath his ribs lies a fierce disease. The sentence is a new statement, and making it a second object of "yahsabun" (they think) is not at all supported by the noble composition, since the fa' in His statement, ﴿So beware of them﴾, is for ordering caution on the basis that they are the greatest of enemies.

﴿Allah destroy them﴾ is an invocation against them and a request from the Essence of the Exalted that He curse them and disgrace them, or it is a teaching to the believers that they should invoke this against them. His statement, exalted is He, ﴿How are they turned away?﴾ is an expression of wonder at their state, that is: how are they turned away from the truth toward what they are upon of disbelief and misguidance?

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 63, verse 5:

﴿And when it is said to them﴾ at the appearance of their wrongdoing, by way of counsel.

﴿"Come, the Messenger of Allah will ask forgiveness for you," they twist their heads﴾ i.e., they turn them aside out of arrogance.

﴿And you see them turning away﴾ they turn away from the one who speaks or from the seeking of forgiveness.

﴿while they are arrogant﴾ (p-253) from that.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 63, verse 6:

﴿It is the same for them whether you seek forgiveness for them﴾ as when they come to you apologizing for their misdeeds. It is also read as "istaghfarta" with the interrogative particle dropped, relying on the indication of "am" (or) to it. It is also read as "a-istaghfarta" with the interrogative hamza prolonged, not by converting the hamzat al-wasl into an alif.

﴿or you do not seek forgiveness for them﴾ as when they persist in their ugly deeds and are too proud to apologize and seek forgiveness.

﴿Allah will never forgive them﴾ ever, because of their persistence in corruption and their firm entrenchment in disbelief.

﴿Indeed, Allah does not guide the people who are defiantly corrupt﴾ those who are thoroughly corrupt, who have stepped outside the circle of reform and are immersed in disbelief and hypocrisy. The intended meaning is either that they are those specific individuals, and the explicit noun is used in place of the pronoun to show the extent of their corruption; or that it refers to the category, in which they are included from the outset.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 63, verse 7:

And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿They are the ones who say﴾, that is, to the Ansar.

﴿Do not spend on those who are with the Messenger of Allah﴾ (ﷺ).

﴿Until they disperse﴾, meaning the poor among the Muhajirun. This is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) that functions as a justification (ta'lil) for their wickedness (fisq), or for Allah's not forgiving them. It has also been read as "until they disperse" (yanfidu), from anfada al-qawm, meaning when the people's provisions have run out. Its literal sense is: it has become time for them to shake out their saddlebags (yanfudu mazawidahum).

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And to Allah belong the treasuries of the heavens and the earth﴾ is a refutation and nullification of what they claimed, namely that their not spending would lead to the poor dispersing from around him (ﷺ). It shows that the treasuries of provision are in the hand of Allah alone; He gives to whom He wills and withholds from whom He wills.

﴿But the hypocrites do not understand﴾. That is due to their ignorance of Allah, Exalted is He, and of His affairs; and for this reason they utter from the sayings of disbelief what they utter.

They say, "If we return to al-Madina, the mightier will surely expel the weaker from it." It is narrated that Jahjah ibn Sa'id, the hired man (ajir) of 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, quarrelled with Sinan al-Juhani, an ally of Ibn Ubayy, and they fought. Jahjah cried out, "O Muhajirun!" and Sinan cried out, "O Ansar!" Some of the poor Muhajirun aided Jahjah, and he slapped Sinan. Sinan complained to Ibn Ubayy, who said to the Ansar, "Do not spend (on them)... etc. By Allah, if we return to al-Madina, the mightier will surely expel the weaker from it." By "the mightier" he meant himself, and by "the weaker" he meant the believers. The attribution of this statement to the hypocrites is because they were pleased with it. So Allah refuted this by His saying: ﴿And might belongs to Allah, to His Messenger, and to the believers﴾, meaning: to Allah belongs dominance and power, and to whomever He has made mighty from among His Messenger and the believers, and not to anyone else.

﴿But the hypocrites do not know﴾, because of their extreme ignorance and delusion, so they utter whatever they utter. It is narrated that when 'Abdullah ibn Ubayy wanted to enter al-Madina, his son 'Abdullah ibn 'Abdullah ibn Ubayy, who was sincere, confronted him and said, "If you do not acknowledge might for Allah and His Messenger, I will surely strike your neck." When he saw his seriousness, he said, "I bear witness that might belongs to Allah, to His Messenger, and to the believers." The Prophet (ﷺ) said to his son, "May Allah reward you well on behalf of His Messenger and the believers."

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 63, verse 9:

﴿O you who have believed, let not your wealth and your children divert you from the remembrance of Allah﴾ That is: let not preoccupation with managing their affairs, attending to their interests, and enjoying them distract you from engaging in the remembrance of Him, mighty and majestic is He, namely the prayer and the other acts of worship mentioned that are due to the One who is worshipped. The intended meaning is the prohibition against being diverted by them, and the prohibition is directed at them (i.e., at wealth and children) for emphasis, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and let not the enmity of a people prompt you to transgress﴾ ... etc. ﴿And whoever does that﴾ That is: diverting oneself with the worldly life away from the religion. ﴿Then those are the losers﴾ That is: the complete ones in loss, since they sold the great and enduring for the petty and perishing.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 63, verse 10:

﴿And spend of that which We have provided for you﴾ i.e., some of what We have given you by way of bounty, without its acquisition being from your own effort for the sake of storing up for the Hereafter.

﴿before death comes to one of you﴾ by witnessing its signs, beholding its indications and its portents. The placing of the object before the subject here is, as has passed many times, for the sake of emphasis on what is placed first and for arousing eagerness for what is deferred.

﴿and he says﴾ upon being certain of its arrival.

﴿"My Lord, if only You would defer me﴾ i.e., grant me respite.

﴿to a near term"﴾ i.e., a short period.

﴿"and I would give charity﴾ in the accusative (naṣb) as an answer to the wish (tamannī). It is also read "fa-atasaddaqa" (fa-ataṣaddaqa).

﴿"and be among the righteous."﴾ In the jussive (jazm), as a conjunction with the grammatical position (maḥall) of "fa-aṣṣaddaqa", as if it were said: "If You defer me, I will give charity and be [among the righteous]." It is also read "wa-akūna" in the accusative, as a conjunction with its wording (lafẓ), and "wa-akūnu" in the nominative, i.e., "and I am going to be, by way of a promise from Him, among the righteous."

﴿And Allah will never delay a soul when its term has come.﴾ That is: He will never grant it respite.

﴿When its term has come.﴾ That is: the last of its lifespan, or its end, if "term" is taken to mean the span of time extending from the beginning of life to its end.

﴿And Allah is Aware of what you do.﴾ So He will recompense you for it: if it is good, then good; and if it is evil, then evil. So hasten to the good deeds and prepare yourselves for what is coming. It is also read as "ya'maluna" (تَعْمَلُونَ with the yā' prefix, i.e., "they do") — with the letter yā' (ياء) pronounced with the dot below, as a yā' of the present tense.

On the authority of the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "Whoever recites Surat al-Munafiqun will be free from hypocrisy (nifaq)."
